answer: In DeepWalk (Perozzi et al., 2014), the context of a vertex v_i is defined as the set of vertices that appear within a window of size w around v_i in short random walks: for each walk, the vertices v_{i-w},...,v_{i+w} (excluding v_i itself) form the context C of v_i, so the skip-gram objective maximizes the log-probability of observing these neighbors given v_i, i.e., minimize -log Pr({v_{i-w},...,v_{i+w}} \ {v_i} | Φ(v_i)). The ordering constraint is that the context vertices are treated as ordered by their position relative to v_i (in the walk). Removing this ordering constraint means the model is trained to predict the context vertices as an unordered set: the probability is factorized independently over context vertices, Pr(C | Φ(v_i)) = ∏_{u∈C} Pr(u | Φ(v_i)), so the output for each context vertex is predicted independently of its position. This makes the training problem simpler and cheaper to optimize (e.g., via hierarchical softmax with a single shared prediction per context vertex, and it is order-invariant), at the cost of discarding positional information within the window.
